title: Odile and the Hymn
premise: Yara Vane takes a teaching post in the hollow town of Odile, where a class of students vanished decades ago and the town still sings a four-verse hymn at every gathering. Yara discovers that the hymn's missing fifth verse, when sung, calls the vanished children home—but they return wrong, hungry for the living to join their choir. Haunted by photographs at their late grandmother's house that keep gaining an extra empty chair, Yara realizes the choir has marked them as its next soloist. With a band of misfit townsfolk—the church organist, a retired sheriff, and a student who survived the last attempt—Yara reconstructs the fifth verse and learns to sing it backwards, a counter-hymn that unbinds the choir and frees the children's ghosts. In the end, Yara chooses to stay in Odile, no longer invisible, as the town buries its hymn and builds a family from the ones who remained.
about_author: Casper Reyes is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent six years in small towns where everyone remembered a tragedy no one would name. They write horror about quiet places, insisting that the scariest songs are the ones a community agrees to sing together.

chapters.title: The Empty Desk Roster
chapters.summary: Yara Vane arrives in Odile to teach at Hollow Creek School and notices the attendance ledger skips an entire year. The principal, Mr. Aldous Fen, warns them to keep the doors counted and the lights on. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: wary optimism curdling into unease.

chapters.title: Twenty-Six Chairs
chapters.summary: On Yara's first day, twenty-seven students file in, but the roster lists twenty-six. No one acknowledges the extra child, who sits perfectly still in the back. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: the first crack in the town's practiced normalcy.

chapters.title: Grandma's Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Sorting their grandmother's house, Yara finds family photographs where an empty wooden chair appears in the background—photos taken years apart, the chair always closer. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: grief tangled with creeping dread.

chapters.title: The Hymn at Wednesday Gathering
chapters.summary: The town gathers to sing the four-verse Odile Hymn. Yara notices the congregation mouths a pause after the fourth verse, a held breath where something should be. Student Marisol Tabb warns them: never hum what you don't know. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: communal warmth with a rotten center.

chapters.title: Marisol Knows the Year
chapters.summary: Marisol, sharp and friendless, tells Yara about the Class of '61, who walked into the woods during rehearsal and never returned. The school sealed their classroom. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: lonely kinship between two outsiders.

chapters.title: The Organist's Confession
chapters.summary: Organist Dell Hargrove, drunk and terrified, admits the fifth verse exists—his mother wrote it before she vanished. He plays four bars and begs Yara to forget them. POV: Dell. Emotional beat: guilt that has fermented for sixty years.

chapters.title: Counting Doors at Midnight
chapters.summary: Yara follows the school's old protocol: lights on, doors counted. At midnight there is one door too many, standing open in a wall with no room behind it. Singing drifts through. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: the rules are real, and they are failing.

chapters.title: The Chair Moves Closer
chapters.summary: In the newest photograph, the chair sits at the dinner table, set for one. Yara's neighbor Ruth, a retired sheriff, recognizes the chair from the missing classroom and finally breaks her silence. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: an old lawwoman choosing conscience over silence.

chapters.title: What the Class of '61 Sang
chapters.summary: Ruth reveals the town's bargain: after the children vanished, the founders wove the hymn into civic life to keep the choir fed and the rest of the town spared. Justice was traded for safety. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: the weight of complicity.

chapters.title: Marisol Hears Her Name in the Verse
chapters.summary: Marisol, humming the recovered fragment, begins sleepwalking toward the woods. Yara finds her at the tree line at 3 a.m., the choir's voices braided with her own. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: terror of being chosen.

chapters.title: Aldous Fen's Ledger
chapters.summary: Yara confronts Fen, who has kept sixty years of rosters—every generation, one name underlined. The underlined names are the choir's soloists, taken one by one. The latest underlined name is Yara Vane. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: betrayal by the person meant to protect them.

chapters.title: The Found Family Pact
chapters.summary: Yara, Marisol, Dell, and Ruth gather in the sealed classroom and swear an oath: no one gets taken alone, and no one gets fed to the song. They name themselves the Odile Five. POV: Dell. Emotional beat: belonging, hard-won and fragile.

chapters.title: Rehearsal in the Sealed Room
chapters.summary: Inside the Class of '61's classroom, chalkboards bear half-erased sheet music. The five reconstruct the fifth verse from chalk ghosts, Dell's memory, and Marisol's dreams. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: dread and exhilaration of forbidden knowledge.

chapters.title: Singing It Backwards
chapters.summary: Dell discovers his mother's marginalia: the verse sung in reverse unmakes the choir instead of feeding it. But reversing it requires four voices who know the first four verses by heart—and one who has heard the fifth. POV: Dell. Emotional beat: hope with a terrible price tag.

chapters.title: The Town Turns Out
chapters.summary: Fen rallies the town against the five, framing them as blasphemers. Neighbors who shared pies now stand on Yara's lawn, humming. The extra child from class appears at every window. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: exile inside one's own home.

chapters.title: Ruth's Last Arrest
chapters.summary: Ruth deputizes herself one final time and arrests Fen for the sixty-one years of sanctioned sacrifice, seizing the ledger as evidence. The town's sheriff's office, long complicit, splits. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: justice outside the law, claimed at last.

chapters.title: The Choir Comes for Marisol
chapters.summary: The choir takes Marisol to the woods to rehearse her solo. The five follow the singing into the dark, where the vanished children stand in rows, faces smoothed like unfinished clay. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: love walking straight into horror.

chapters.title: The First Voice Falters
chapters.summary: The counter-hymn begins in the woods. The children stir; the choir's true shape—a vast, patient thing wearing sixty years of voices—turns its attention on the singers. Ruth's verse falters; the hymn gains on them. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: courage failing at the worst moment.

chapters.title: Marisol's Solo, Reversed
chapters.summary: Marisol, marked as soloist, becomes the weapon: she sings the fifth verse backwards from inside the choir, her voice cutting the mass of voices apart. The children's true faces return, one by one. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: the smallest voice doing the largest work.

chapters.title: The Unmaking at Dawn
chapters.summary: The choir unravels at first light, the fifth verse dissolving into ordinary birdsong. Fen, hearing his mother's voice among the freed dead, walks into the last of the music and is gone. The woods fall silent. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: victory shadowed by cost.

chapters.title: Burying the Hymn
chapters.summary: The town, hollowed and ashamed, gathers one last time—not to sing, but to bury the hymn's sheet music beside the Class of '61's memorial. Names are read aloud for the first time. The extra chair in the photographs is gone. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: grief transformed into reckoning.

chapters.title: Staying
chapters.summary: Yara could leave; the road out is finally open. Instead they stay, adopting a found family of the four who sang with them, and reopen the sealed classroom as a real room for real children. The last photograph shows five chairs, all of them full. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: belonging, chosen and earned.
